acts.head: Demand shifts. The order policy lags behind.
acts.sub: In a seasonal demand test with a 4-week lead time, a standard base-stock policy took 26.3 weeks to settle after each change in demand.

acts.head: Each re-forecast's change gets thrown away.
acts.sub: Planners re-forecast every week, but the order policy reads only the newest number. How far the forecast just moved, an early sign of a shift, goes unused.

acts.head: Read the forecast changes. Seasonal cost falls 72%.
acts.sub: An AI ordering policy reads recent forecast changes and a shift alarm, then adjusts a base-stock order. Cost: 116.8 to 32.5. Settling: 9.8 weeks.

acts.head: Best where demand really shifts.
acts.sub: On seven real Walmart items picked for shifting demand, cost fell 4.2% to 23.0%. On stable items, expect little gain. On sparse demand, a rival AI method won.

post.linkedin:
Your forecast already tells you when demand is shifting: in how much it moved since last week. A new study feeds that movement into the ordering decision and cuts cost 4.2% to 23.0% on seven real Walmart items.

New open-access research in Operations Research Perspectives, from authors at Constructor University in Bremen, tests an AI ordering policy that reads the recent history of forecast revisions plus a shift alarm, and adjusts a standard base-stock order up or down.

In a simulated seasonal test, cost falls 72% against an adaptive base-stock policy (116.8 to 32.5), and the time to settle after a change drops from 26.3 to 9.8 weeks. The edge grows with lead time: level with a rival AI method at 4 weeks, 13.8% ahead of it at 8.

The limits: the Walmart items were picked for strongly shifting demand, and on stable items the authors expect little gain. On sparse, lumpy demand a rival AI method did better. No company has run it live.

Does your replenishment logic ever look at how the forecast changed, or only at the latest number?
